nameStory: The 'netted iris' gets its name from the distinctive net-like pattern of fibers that covers its bulbs, looking like tiny fishing nets wrapped around the base. This reticulated (net-patterned) covering is so characteristic that it gives the plant its scientific name 'reticulata,' from the Latin word for 'netted.'
description: Netted iris is a tiny early-blooming bulb flower that stands just 4-6 inches tall when in bloom. It produces delicate, fragrant iris flowers in shades of deep blue-purple with bright yellow and white markings, appearing in late winter or very early spring. The narrow, grass-like leaves emerge after the flowers and can grow taller than the blooms. This miniature iris is originally from mountainous regions and is grown as an ornamental garden plant that has occasionally escaped cultivation.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Classic iris shape but tiny - only 2-3 inches across with three upright petals (standards) and three drooping petals (falls) marked with bright yellow and white streaks that smell sweetly fragrant

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Very narrow, grass-like leaves that are square in cross-section and feel stiff between your fingers, emerging after the flowers and growing 8-12 inches tall

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Extremely short when flowering - you might walk right past these diminutive plants that barely peek above the ground in early spring

idTips.label: Bulb
idTips.description: Small bulb covered in a distinctive net-like fibrous coating that feels papery and looks like brown mesh wrapping - visible if you dig carefully around the base

habitat: Found occasionally in cultivated gardens, rock gardens, and naturalized areas where it has escaped from cultivation. Prefers well-drained, sandy or rocky soils and full sun to partial shade. Most commonly spotted in residential areas and botanical gardens rather than wild natural areas.

seasonality.spring: Flowers appear in very early spring, often while snow is still on the ground, followed by the emergence of narrow leaves that continue growing through late spring.
seasonality.summer: Leaves remain green through early summer, then die back completely as the plant goes dormant underground.
seasonality.fall: Completely dormant with no visible parts above ground - the bulb rests underground preparing for next year's early show.
seasonality.winter: No visible growth above ground, though flower buds may begin emerging from soil in late winter during warm spells.

funFact: This tiny iris is one of the earliest flowers to bloom in New England, often pushing up through snow and blooming when temperatures are still below freezing - the flowers can actually survive being covered by fresh snowfall and pop back up when it melts!
confusionNotes: Could be mistaken for crocuses when not in bloom, but netted iris leaves are distinctively square in cross-section and much narrower than crocus leaves. The classic three-petaled iris flower shape is unmistakable once you see it.
contextualKnowledge: Though called 'netted iris,' this species is also known as 'snow iris' for its remarkably early blooming time. It's not native to New England but originates from mountainous regions of Turkey and the Caucasus, explaining its cold tolerance.
compareHints: Unlike New England's native blue flag irises which are tall wetland plants, netted iris is tiny and prefers dry, well-drained soils. It's much smaller than any other iris in the region and blooms months earlier than native species. The miniature size and extremely early bloom time make it unique among regional irises.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Northern blue flag is much larger and more robust than slender blue flag, which has narrow, grass-like leaves and smaller flowers.
Yellow iris is the only consistently yellow-flowered iris you'll find growing wild in New England wetlands - all our native iris species like northern blue flag have blue or purple flowers.
Japanese Iris differs from Northern Blue Flag by its gray-green (rather than bright green) leaves and reddish-purple flower tones instead of pure blue-purple.
Slender blue flag is much more delicate than the common northern blue flag, with leaves that are dramatically narrower (pencil-width vs.

Unlike its freshwater-loving cousins like northern blue flag (which grows in marshes and pond edges), beach-head iris is the only New England iris that can survive in pure beach sand with constant salt exposure.
Dwarf crested iris is dramatically smaller than all other New England irises - while northern blue flag and yellow iris tower at 2-4 feet tall in wetlands, this woodland species stays under 6 inches.
Compared to northern blue flag, southern blue flag typically has broader, more rounded flower petals and slightly wider leaves.
Unlike other New England irises that have blue, purple, or yellow flowers, blackberry lily is the only one with orange, spotted blooms.
Sweet iris differs from New England's native blue flag irises by its sweet fragrance and slightly more purple-tinted flowers.
Siberian iris differs from Northern Blue Flag by having much narrower, more grass-like leaves and more compact growth, while Yellow Iris has broader leaves and bright yellow flowers.
Japanese iris differs from native blue flags by its massive, completely flat flowers and preference for consistently wet, acidic soil.
Unlike our common northern blue flag with its blue-purple flowers or the invasive yellow iris with bright yellow blooms, cemetery iris stands out with pure white flowers.
